summary: The Orthodox Confession of Peter Mogila teaches that the Eucharist is the Body and Blood of Christ under the species of bread and wine, in which Christ is present really and properly. At the consecration the priest invokes the Holy Spirit and the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the substance of Christ's body and blood, so that the bread becomes the very Body of Christ and the wine his very Blood, with only the appearances remaining. Only a lawfully ordained priest may celebrate it, and it is given to clergy and laity in both kinds. The confession also says the mystery is offered as a sacrifice for all orthodox Christians, living and dead, and calls it a propitiation as well as a commemoration of Christ's death.

points.question: What happens to the bread and wine?
points.answer: By the working of the Holy Spirit, called down on the gifts, the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the very substance of Christ's body and blood; only the visible species remain, so that the body is received by faith.

points.question: Is it a sacrifice?
points.answer: Yes. The priest offers the unbloody sacrifice, and the mystery is offered as a sacrifice for all orthodox Christians, living and dead. Its fruits include a commemoration of Christ's death and a propitiation for sins of the living and the dead.

points.question: Who may administer and receive?
points.answer: Only a lawfully ordained priest may administer it, even in urgent need. Clergy and laity alike receive both the bread and the wine.
